extracted.intended_audience: novelists, writers of fiction, and critics studying the craft of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling a novel’s point of view and its modes of treatment (dramatic/scene vs pictorial/retrospect), and on how to deploy scenes, narration, and authorial voice to serve the subject. Focuses on practical trade-offs and techniques for developing a story’s presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic (scenic) method / enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the reader at the angle of vision so the story is enacted 'by its look and behaviour at particular moments' rather than reported by a narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic stories are strictly scenic: one episode follows another with no reflective summary; they admit no private access to characters' minds, transmuting thoughts and motives into action. This form gives weight, compactness and authority and is 'the most finished form that fiction can take.' Use it where the subject can be treated scenically and when the sharpest, most immediate effect is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to subject (subject dictates method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose dramatization vs pictorial narration according to what the subject demands; 'the subject dictates the method.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatization is inappropriate where the story's burden lies within a particular consciousness (study of a soul, growth of a character) or where the story is too large or panoramic to be treated solely as scenes. Conversely, where a subject 'will tell itself in perfect rightness' scenically, prefer dramatic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial / retrospective narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a narrator (author or person in the book) to gather experience and create a composed impression of events as a reflection of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictorial books involve a point of view that is not the reader’s; they suit subjects needing general or panoramic survey, accumulated impressions over time, or accounts that cannot be wholly enacted moment-to-moment. The natural form is recall, meditation and summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dramatic technique inside a pictorial framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind of the narrator can become the stage so that 'the shapes of thought in the man’s mind tell their own story'—i.e., enactment can occur within a reflective narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible let reactions and moments perform the scene inside the narrator's consciousness so the narrator's voice recedes and the reader's point of view is restored. This allows pictorial narratives to gain immediacy without abandoning their retrospective advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration required for breadth of time and accumulated events
rubrics_metrics.description: Where much has happened (e.g., a year in a man's life) too much exists to be wholly acted; an account from the narrator is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narration/summary when the story covers long periods, many memories, or material that cannot economically be dramatized scene by scene. Balance summaries with enacted moments for economy and salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: First person vs third person (temporal and authorial freedoms)
rubrics_metrics.description: First person fixes the point of view unambiguously (the narrator's own perspective) but limits temporal flexibility; third person allows the author temporal freedom and the ability to range between retrospective and immediate tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose first person for a strictly bounded, intimate field of vision. Choose third person (including oblique/reporting third) when you want to keep a character’s perspective but also allow shifts in time (near/past) and subtle authorial reinforcement or supplementation of the character’s vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique narration / blended authorial presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the seeing-eye of a character while allowing the author's mind to 'look over his shoulder' so the picture contains more than any single consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oblique narration blends the character’s voice with the author's, making the narrator's voice less insistent while retaining a fixed point of view. This can deepen the impression, add information beyond the character's perception, and avoid blurring focus if handled subtly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermittent objective treatment of the seer
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally 'close' the seer’s consciousness so he becomes impenetrable and can be presented as an object among other people—this sharpens his dramatic presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without violating the chosen method, the author may suspend the focal character’s inner access so the character can 'mingle with the rest' and be given conversational or dramatic weight like other figures. Use this device to prevent the central consciousness from dissolving into a 'luminous blur' and to give it solidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of pure first-person reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: A story rigidly told from one actor’s first-person point of view denies the full unmixed effect of drama and mixes report with enacted scenes awkwardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure first-person narration makes true drama impossible because the actor who reports cannot present the scene with the same crispness as direct enactment. If dramatic immediacy is required, consider oblique or third-person strategies that permit more direct scene presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'minstrel’s licence' unless fully justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling the story as the author’s unmediated voice (the easy way) reduces the author’s need for disciplined method and is typically inferior unless the writer can sustain it without losing the story’s strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve the explicitly authorial, unbounded narrator only for writers who can make it seem to lose none of the advantages of more cautious styles; otherwise choose a more disciplined point of view tailored to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a disciplined method to make the most of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The only effective approach is a 'choice and disciplined method' that makes the most of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early how far to dramatize, when to summarize, and how to handle point of view; let the subject and desired effects guide consistent application of technique rather than ad hoc shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy and strategic use of the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incident, the scene, is the chief instrument of the novelist and should be the prime concern in placing action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the scene produces the sharpest effect, use it where emphasis must fall. But use it prudently: do not waste scenes on material better served by summary; prepare scenes so they can act economically and achieve decisive climactic or demonstrative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the scene’s limitations (time/space and cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene cannot foreshorten time or space: as the reader sees it, it displays the whole time and space it occupies; thus scenes are 'expensive' in terms of narrative time and length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting scenes do work unsuited to them (covering long stretches, providing panoramic survey). Prepare scenes in advance with supporting narrative so they can operate swiftly and sharply; otherwise the scene will be overtaxed and lose force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture (panoramic survey) as subordinate and complementary to drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture provides command of time and space and accumulates impressions over periods; its office is preparatory and complementary to drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial passages to travel over periods, pile up impressions, and supply what drama lacks (scope, economy). Then deploy scenes to 'complete' those impressions with sharp visibility and action. Keep picture and drama to their natural functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert pictorial weakness into strength by dramatizing the narrator’s mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging that pictorial report may seem 'thin and flat,' the author can make the mirror (the narrator’s mind) a visible object and dramatize it—thus turning disability into a new strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When telling is inevitable, make the telling itself lively and dramatic by focusing on the mind doing the remembering—its reactions, voice, and internal drama—so the reflective method yields powerful effects of its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: do not squander scenes or gratuitously break into dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overusing dramatic presentation when it gains nothing; novelists often 'squander the scene' by breaking into dialogue where there is no definite gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve dialogue and dramatic enactment for moments that require them; do not use them as a default. A fully wrought, unified scene that gathers many issues and advances the story is rare and valuable—seek to create it rather than many thin scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the technical aspects of craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism and good writing require examination of how books are made; technical familiarity with modes of rendering (scene, picture, panoramic survey) is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read constructively and study the workmanship of many novels to understand the relative uses of different means. Writers and critics should learn the craft by following the process and recreating books for themselves rather than relying on vague generalities about authors' talents.
